A2

Words: 213 Articles: 1
2013 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 213
A2 OurBigBook.com
A monic quadratic polynomial over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root in that field. Testing the nine choices of its two coefficients in F3​ gives
x2+1,x2+x+2,x2+2x+2.​
(1)
For clarity, a zero constant term gives a root at zero. Among constant term one, only the zero linear coefficient avoids roots at 1,2. Among constant term two, precisely the linear coefficients one and two avoid roots. This exhausts all choices.
Put f=x4+x+2. Its values at 0,1,2 are respectively 2,1,2, so it has no linear factor. If this quartic were reducible, absence of a linear factor would force a factorization into two irreducible quadratics. Division by the three candidates above gives remainders respectively x,x+1,x+1, all nonzero. Thus f is an irreducible polynomial.
The quotient by an irreducible polynomial is a field consequently gives a field of 34=81 elements. Its nonzero elements form a multiplicative group of a finite field of order 80. In this field, a4=1+2a. Successive squaring gives
a8=1+a+a2,a16=2+a+2a3.
(2)
The latter is not one: otherwise the nonzero polynomial 1+x+2x3 of degree below four would vanish at a, contradicting its minimal polynomial. By Lagrange's theorem, (a16)5=a80=1. Since five is prime, its order is exactly five. Hence one answer is
ζ=2+a+2a3.​
(3)
Its other nonidentity powers are the remaining primitive fifth roots. It is unnecessary to prove that a itself generates the entire multiplicative group.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
The orbit of s is Os​={gs:g∈G}, and its stabilizer is Gs​={g∈G:gs=s}. The identity fixes s; if g,h fix it then (gh)s=g(hs)=s; and gs=s implies g−1s=s. Thus Gs​ is a subgroup.
A group action is transitive when it has just one orbit: for every s,t∈S there is g∈G with gs=t.

b

Words: 43 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 43
b OurBigBook.com
On the set of left cosets G/H, define g⋅(xH)=(gx)H. Given xH and yH, the element yx−1 sends the first to the second. Thus the coset action is transitive. In particular the orbit of H is the entire coset space, and its stabilizer is H.

c

Words: 119 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 119
c OurBigBook.com
Two group actions on S1​,S2​ are equivalent if there is a bijection ϕ:S1​→S2​ such that ϕ(gs)=gϕ(s) for all g,s. Such a bijection is equivariant.
The orbit-stabilizer theorem in this form says that the action on Os​ is equivalent to the left coset action on G/Gs​, by gGs​↦gs. This map is well-defined and injective because gs=hs exactly when h−1g∈Gs​, and it is onto by the definition of the orbit. It is equivariant by multiplication.
Thus every transitive action is a coset action. Two such actions G/H and G/K are equivalent exactly when H,K are conjugate: stabilizers at different points of one orbit are conjugate, and a conjugacy explicitly supplies a coset-action equivalence. This last classification is what makes counting by orbit types possible.

i

Words: 114 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 114
i OurBigBook.com
A cyclic group of order six has exactly one subgroup of each order 1,2,3,6, and no others. Since it is abelian, these are also its four conjugacy classes of subgroups. Thus there is one transitive group action of each size 1,2,3,6.
An action on six points is a disjoint union of its orbits. Its equivalence type is therefore determined by nonnegative integers satisfying
n1​+2n2​+3n3​+6n6​=6.
(4)
If n6​=1 there is one possibility. If n6​=0, the possibilities n3​=0,1,2 allow respectively 4,2,1 choices of n2​, with n1​ then fixed. Hence
1+4+2+1=8 inequivalent actions.​
(5)
This is counting finite group actions by transitive orbit types. Equivalently, a generator acts as a permutation whose cycles have lengths dividing six, and these are its eight possible cycle types on six points.

ii

Words: 90 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 90
ii OurBigBook.com
The symmetric group S3​ has subgroups of orders 1,2,3,6. There is one trivial subgroup, three conjugate subgroups generated by transpositions, one order-three subgroup A3​, and the whole group. These are all subgroups by Lagrange's theorem. Thus again there is one conjugacy class for each index 6,3,2,1.
The coset action classification in part (c) supplies exactly one transitive orbit type of each of these sizes. The same orbit-multiplicity equation as in part (i) applies, giving
8 inequivalent actions.​
(6)
The equality of the two counts comes from their identical lists of transitive orbit types, rather than from the groups being isomorphic.

(a/p)∈{0,1,−1}.​
(7)

(−1/p)=(−1)(p−1)/2={1,−1,​p≡1(mod4),p≡3(mod4).​​

(ab/p)=(a/p)(b/p).​

For distinct odd primes p,q, the quadratic reciprocity law is
(p/q)(q/p)=(−1)2p−1​2q−1​.​
(11)
Thus the two symbols have opposite signs exactly when both primes are three modulo four; otherwise they agree. Distinctness excludes zero symbols.

b OurBigBook.com
Factor a=∏i​qi​ and b=∏j​pj​, listing prime factors with repetitions. Coprimality ensures qi​=pj​. By the definition of the Jacobi symbol and multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol,
(a/b)(b/a)=∏i,j​(qi​/pj​)(pj​/qi​)=(−1)(∑i​(qi​−1)/2)(∑j​(pj​−1)/2).
(12)
For odd integers r,s,
2rs−1​≡2r−1​+2s−1​(mod2),
(13)
since the difference is (r−1)(s−1)/2, an even integer. Inductively the two sums in the exponent are congruent to (a−1)/2 and (b−1)/2 modulo two. Hence
(a/b)(b/a)=(−1)2a−1​2b−1​.​
(14)
If either number is one, the empty product convention proves the same identity. This extends the prime law to arbitrary coprime positive odd denominators.

Words: 112
c OurBigBook.com
Put p=4272943. Since p≡7(mod8), the supplementary laws give (−1/p)=−1 and (2/p)=1. Therefore (−286/p)=−(143/p).
Both 143 and p are three modulo four. Reciprocity for the Jacobi symbol, followed by the supplied remainder, gives
(143/p)=−(p/143)=−(103/143).
(15)
Again both denominators are three modulo four, so
(103/143)=−(143/103)=−(40/103).
(16)
Now 103≡7(mod8) and 40=8⋅5. Consequently
(40/103)=(2/103)3(5/103)=(103/5)=(3/5)=−1,
(17)
because the nonzero squares modulo five are one and four. Thus (103/143)=1, (143/p)=−1, and finally
(−286/p)=1.​
(18)
The congruence is soluble, with exactly two distinct solutions modulo this prime: a nonzero root and its negative. The computation uses a prime denominator in its final step; a positive Jacobi symbol with composite denominator would not by itself imply solubility.

The monotone convergence theorem states that if 0≤hn​↑h pointwise for measurable functions, then h is measurable and ∫h=limn​∫hn​, allowing infinity.
Apply it to the partial sums SN​=∑n=0N​fn​. They are nonnegative, measurable, and increase pointwise to f. Finite additivity of the integral and monotone convergence yield
∫R​f=N→∞lim​n=0∑N​∫R​fn​=n=0∑∞​∫R​fn​.​
(19)
The assumed finite sum of integrals makes f integrable. This proves the series-integration rule needed below directly from the stated theorem, without assuming an additional interchange theorem.

For α>0, integration by parts on [0,R] gives
∫0R​xe−αxdx=α21​−e−αR(αR​+α21​).
(20)
The exponential remainder tends to zero. Since the integrand is nonnegative, the monotone convergence theorem applied to truncations identifies the improper integral with the Lebesgue integral. Therefore
∫0∞​xe−αxdx=α−2.​
(21)
Its finite value proves integrability as well as evaluating it.

For x>0, the geometric series gives
1−e−xxe−αx​=∑n=0∞​xe−(n+α)x.
(22)
Every summand is nonnegative and has integral (n+α)−2 by part (a). This numerical series converges by comparison with ∑n≥1​n−2. The series-integration rule proved above therefore yields
∫0∞​1−e−xxe−αx​dx=n=0∑∞​(n+α)21​<∞.​
(23)
The value at the single endpoint zero does not affect this Lebesgue integral.

c OurBigBook.com
On 0<x<1, the geometric expansion gives summands hn​(x)=xn+β−1−xn−β. Their integrals are
∫01​hn​(x)dx=n+β1​−n+1−β1​=n2+n+β−β21−2β​.
(24)
Both powers are integrable because 0<β<1. If β<1/2, each hn​ is nonnegative, since its first exponent is smaller. Their integrals form a convergent nonnegative series: the n=0 term is finite and subsequent terms are bounded by a constant times n−2. The proved series-integration rule applies.
If β>1/2, apply precisely that rule to −hn​, which are nonnegative, and negate the result. At β=1/2 all summands and the integrand are zero. Thus in every case the integral is absolutely integrable and
∫01​1−xxβ−1−x−β​dx=n=0∑∞​n2+n+β−β21−2β​.​
(25)
The common sign of the summands is the reason no unproved theorem for integrating arbitrary signed series is needed.

A null set E⊆R has Lebesgue outer measure zero. Equivalently, for every ϵ>0 it can be covered by countably many open intervals whose total length is less than ϵ. This definition also applies before assuming E measurable; every such set is Lebesgue measurable with measure zero.

A property holds almost everywhere when its exceptional set, where the property fails, is a null set. The exceptional set need not be empty or countable.

Let N be the vector subspace of integrable functions that vanish almost everywhere. The Lebesgue space is the quotient vector space L1(R)=L1(R)/N: its elements are equivalence classes of functions equal almost everywhere. Addition and scalar multiplication are [f]+[g]=[f+g] and c[f]=[cf].
Set ∥[f]∥1​=∫∣f∣. This is well-defined because replacing f by an equal-almost-everywhere representative does not change the integral. It is nonnegative, homogeneous, and obeys the triangle inequality by ∣f+g∣≤∣f∣+∣g∣. Part (i) says its only zero element is the zero class. Hence it is a norm on L1.

If A is closed and an​∈A converges to x∈X, then x cannot lie in the open complement: an open ball about such an x would eventually contain all an​ while missing A. Thus x∈A.
Conversely, suppose A contains every limit of a sequence in A. If x∈A, every ball B(x,1/n) meets A; choose an​ in that intersection. Then an​→x, so x∈A. Hence A=A, proving that a subset of a metric space is a closed set exactly when it is sequentially closed.

Solution

A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence in it converges to a point of that space. A sequence is Cauchy when, for each ϵ>0, there is N such that d(xm​,xn​)<ϵ whenever m,n≥N. The requirement that the limit lie in the space distinguishes completeness from having limits only in a larger ambient space.

Solution

If A is closed in the complete ambient metric space, any Cauchy sequence in A converges in X by completeness, and its limit belongs to A by part (i). Thus A is complete with its restricted metric.
Conversely, suppose A is complete and a sequence an​∈A converges in X to x. A convergent sequence is Cauchy, also in the restricted metric, so completeness of A gives an​→a for some a∈A. Uniqueness of a metric limit gives x=a∈A. Part (i) now makes A closed. Hence
A complete⟺A closed in X.​
(30)

The limit is bounded but does not have finite support. Thus the finite-support subspace is not closed in X, and by part (a)(iii) it is not complete. Equivalently, the displayed sequence is Cauchy in that subspace but has no limit there.

Since the fixed sequence a(m) converges, it is Cauchy, so for sufficiently large j,k its coordinate difference is below ϵ/3. Then
∣aj​−ak​∣≤∣aj​−aj(m)​∣+∣aj(m)​−ak(m)​∣+∣ak(m)​−ak​∣<ϵ.
(31)
Thus a is a Cauchy sequence of real numbers and converges by completeness of R. Hence a∈C, so C is closed. Part (a)(iii) proves the convergent-sequence subspace is complete.

A topological space is compact if every open cover of it has a finite subcover. That is, if X=⋃i∈I​Ui​ with all Ui​ open, finitely many of those same open sets already cover X.

If the intersection were empty, the open complements X∖Fi​ would cover the compact space. A finite subcover would give an empty finite intersection of the corresponding Fi​. But the sets are nested, so any finite intersection is the set with largest index, which is nonempty. This contradiction proves
i⋂​Fi​=∅.​
(32)
This is the nested-closed-set form of the finite intersection property for compact spaces.

Fi​⊆Ufor every i≥N.​

Thus Wdz=Wdz, and ∣W∣2dz=W2dz. Substitution proves Blasius force theorem:

Because σ1​>σ0​, this is strictly increasing in S. The Neyman-Pearson lemma therefore selects an upper-tail rejection region. Under the null, S/σ02​∼χn2​, so size α is obtained with
C={S≥kα​},kα​=σ02​Fn−1​(1−α).​
(85)
Continuity of the chi-squared distribution makes the boundary have probability zero. This is a fixed-mean normal variance test.

Yes, it is a uniformly most powerful test for the one-sided alternative. For every fixed σ12​>σ02​, the likelihood ratio is increasing in the same statistic S. The size-α threshold found in part (c) depends only on the null variance and α, not on the selected alternative variance. Thus one and the same test is most powerful against each simple member of the composite alternative, which is exactly uniform most powerfulness.

At a true variance σ2>0, S/σ2∼χn2​. Therefore the power function is
w(σ2)=1−Fn​(σ2σ02​​Fn−1​(1−α)).​
(86)
The argument of Fn​ decreases as σ2 increases. Since the chi-squared density is positive on the positive half-line, the power is continuous and strictly increasing, with
w(0+)=0,w(σ02​)=α,w(∞)=1.​
(87)
These features determine the requested rough sketch. The curve passes through the size at the null value and approaches one for very large variance.

Solution

Words: 62
a OurBigBook.com
Ignoring a factor independent of the probabilities, the likelihood function is L(π)=∏i​πini​​, so its log is ℓ(π)=∑i​ni​logπi​ subject to ∑i​πi​=1. A Lagrange multiplier gives ni​/πi​=λ. Summing πi​=ni​/λ makes λ=n.
Thus
πi​=ni​/n.​
(88)
Since all counts are positive, a zero fitted cell probability would have zero likelihood. On the interior the log-likelihood is strictly concave, so this stationary point is its unique global maximum.

b

Words: 146 Articles: 1
O5 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 146
b OurBigBook.com
The unrestricted likelihood is maximized at the empirical proportions, while the null likelihood is maximized at πi​(θ). Twice the log of their ratio is
Λ(θ)=2i∑​ni​lognπi​(θ)ni​​.​
(89)
Large values mean the fitted null likelihood is much smaller than the unrestricted maximum, so rejection is in the upper tail.
For a regular identifiable scalar parameter lying in the interior, positive true cell probabilities, and sufficiently large expected counts, Wilks theorem gives an approximate chi-squared distribution with (k−1)−1=k−2 degrees of freedom under the null. The unrestricted probability vector has dimension k−1 and the fitted null has dimension one. At significance level α, reject if Λ(θ)>Fk−2−1​(1−α), or report the approximate p-value 1−Fk−2​(Λ).
Cells with very small expected counts may require a prespecified pooling scheme or simulation calibration; the asymptotic reference is not an exact finite-sample law. For a regular null with d fitted parameters, the corresponding degrees of freedom are k−1−d.

For a fully specified parameter value, do not maximize within the null. Substitute θ0​ directly:
Λ(θ0​)=2i∑​ni​lognπi​(θ0​)ni​​.​
(90)
Under the same regularity and large-count conditions, compare with χk−12​, since no null parameter has been estimated. Reject in its upper tail at the desired significance level. Fixing the parameter increases the reference degrees of freedom by one relative to part (b).

The final cell is a grouped tail. Thus use twelve probabilities
pi​(θ)=e−θi!θi​(0≤i≤10),p11​(θ)=Pθ​(X≥11)=1−∑i=010​pi​(θ).
(91)
Maximize the grouped Grouped Poisson likelihood
ℓ(θ)=∑i=010​ni​logpi​(θ)+n11​logp11​(θ),
(92)
then take πi​=pi​(θ)​ for all twelve cells. For example, the interior likelihood equation is
∑i=010​ni​(θi​−1)+n11​p11​(θ)p10​(θ)​=0,
(93)
because p11′​(θ)=p10​(θ). It can be solved numerically, with no numerical work required here.
It would be incorrect to treat the last six observations as exactly eleven. If the underlying ungrouped particle counts were available, their sample mean would be the usual Poisson maximum likelihood estimate. For the data as supplied, the grouped likelihood handles the unknown tail counts directly.

Words: 88 Articles: 1

ii OurBigBook.com
There are twelve cells and one fitted parameter, so the likelihood-ratio reference is approximately χ102​. The supplied value gives
p-value≈1−F10​(14)=0.18.​
(94)
Thus do not reject the Poisson goodness-of-fit model at the conventional 5% level; it would also not be rejected at 10%. The data do not provide strong evidence of a departure from this model. This is a compatibility conclusion, not proof that the Poisson model is true. A fully specified Poisson mean would instead use eleven degrees of freedom, which is not the fitted situation here.

a OurBigBook.com
With the weighted inner product ⟨p,q⟩w​=∫−11​p(x)q(x)w(x)dx, a family of orthogonal polynomials has degpj​=j, each pj​ nonzero, and
⟨pj​,pk​⟩w​=0(j=k).​
(95)
Continuity and positivity of the weight make the integral finite and give ⟨pj​,pj​⟩w​>0. Unit norm or monic leading coefficient is an additional optional normalization.

b

Words: 68 Articles: 1
P3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 68
b OurBigBook.com
The weight is even, so opposite-parity polynomials are automatically orthogonal. Set p0​=1, p1​=x, then subtract lower-degree components within each parity class. The needed moments are
μ0​=38​,μ2​=1516​,μ4​=3524​.
(96)
Thus p2​=x2−μ2​/μ0​=x2−2/5 is orthogonal to p0​, and p3​=x3−(μ4​/μ2​)x=x3−9x/14 is orthogonal to p1​. Parity supplies every other pair. One valid answer is
p0​=1,p1​=x,p2​=x2−52​,p3​=x3−149​x.​
(97)
All have the required degree and positive norm; arbitrary nonzero rescalings are equally valid.

c

Words: 109 Articles: 1
P3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 109
c OurBigBook.com
The degree-zero polynomial is constant and therefore even. Assume inductively that pj​(−x)=(−1)jpj​(x) for j<k. Define qk​(x)=(−1)kpk​(−x), which has the same leading coefficient as pk​.
Changing variable x↦−x and using the even weight and inductive hypothesis gives ⟨qk​,pj​⟩w​=(−1)k+j⟨pk​,pj​⟩w​=0 for j<k. Hence qk​−pk​ has degree below k and is orthogonal to every p0​,…,pk−1​. Those polynomials form a basis for the polynomials of degree below k, so the difference is orthogonal to itself. Positivity of the weighted inner product forces it to be zero.
Therefore
pk​(−x)=(−1)kpk​(x),​
(98)
completing the induction and proving parity of orthogonal polynomials for an even weight. Thus even indices give even functions and odd indices give odd functions, regardless of the nonzero normalization chosen.

A real square matrix is orthogonal when QTQ=I, equivalently when its columns form an orthonormal basis. Taking determinants gives (detQ)2=1, so
detQ∈{1,−1}.​
(99)
In particular it is invertible with inverse QT and preserves the Euclidean norm.

b

Words: 44 Articles: 1
P4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 44
b OurBigBook.com
A QR decomposition is A=QR​ with Q orthogonal and R upper triangular. One algorithm for computing it is Householder reflection reduction; a sequence of such reflections produces a QR factorization. The diagonal of R may include zero when A is singular, and no nonsingularity assumption is needed here.

Comparing the jth columns of A=QR gives aj​=Qrj​. Thus
∥aj​∥2=rjT​QTQrj​=rjT​rj​=∥rj​∥2.
(100)
Taking nonnegative square roots proves ∥aj​∥=∥rj​∥​. This is simply norm preservation by an orthogonal matrix.

Use a QR factorization, whose existence is supplied. Since ∣detQ∣=1 and R is triangular,
∣detA∣=∣detR∣=∏j=1n​∣rjj​∣.
(101)
Each diagonal entry is one component of its column, so ∣rjj​∣≤∥rj​∥=∥aj​∥. Multiplication yields Hadamard determinant inequality:
∣detA∣≤j=1∏n​∥aj​∥.​
(102)
The argument includes singular matrices, since a zero diagonal factor makes the determinant zero.

Every column has n entries of magnitude at most one, so ∥aj​∥2≤n. Substituting in part (d) gives
∣detA∣≤j=1∏n​n​=nn/2.​
(103)
The bound comes from the maximum allowed column lengths, together with Hadamard's inequality.
